query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys in the form of nanoscale thin films or lithographically patterned nanoribbons, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles, given that the notable response reported for bulk forms may not persist in a genuinely low-dimensional state and that heat-transfer rate limits cycle frequency? Specify one controlled intervention, predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, applicable operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy thin films, increasing interfacial constraints and reduced domain size suppress the magnetostructural transformation that underlies the bulk magnetocaloric response, leading to diminished adiabatic temperature changes and enhanced hysteresis, which can be partially restored by increasing the film thickness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films (20 nm) on a substrate without additional layers.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the film thickness in discrete steps (e.g., 20, 50, 100, 200 nm) while keeping composition and deposition conditions fixed.
generation.conditions: Measure magnetocaloric properties in low applied fields up to ~2 T over 80–350 K during cycling at varying frequencies to assess changes in ΔTad (or ΔS) and hysteresis.
generation.structural_mediator: Finite-size and interfacial constraints affecting the magnetostructural transformation and domain-wall mobility.
generation.mechanism: As the film thickness increases, strain relaxation and reduced interface-to-volume ratio enhance the cooperative magnetic transitions, thereby increasing the magnetocaloric effect and reducing hysteresis compared with thinner as-deposited films.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thicker films display larger isothermal entropy changes and smaller hysteresis losses, restoring a more bulk-like magnetocaloric performance under low-field cycling compared to the highly constrained 20 nm baseline.
generation.baseline: Magnetocaloric response measurements of the 20 nm as-deposited thin film at 80–350 K and up to ~2 T.
generation.boundary: Valid for thicknesses in the nominal range of 20–200 nm, under magnetic fields ≤2 T, from ~80–350 K. Extrapolation beyond these thicknesses or field strengths may be inaccurate due to untested structural transitions.
generation.uncertainty: Influence of residual stress or small shifts in composition with thickness may alter magnetocaloric trends and remain insufficiently quantified with current data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a thickness series (20, 50, 100, 200 nm) of FeMnNiGeSi thin films on identical substrates using the same sputtering conditions, then measure magnetocaloric effects and hysteresis via magnetometry and microcalorimetry under cycling up to 2 T at multiple frequencies and temperatures between 80–350 K.
measurements: Estimate isothermal entropy change (ΔS) over 80–350 K for each thickness.
Quantify hysteresis from M–H loops and calorimetric data at various cycle rates.
Analyze microstructure (grain size, interface density, stress state) via XRD and microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Observation of uniform magnetocaloric values and hysteresis across all film thicknesses—i.e., absence of any thickness dependence—would falsify the proposed mechanism that interfacial constraints and finite-size effects degrade the low-field magnetocaloric response and boost hysteresis.

cited_evidence.text: Relative cooling powers (RCP) for equivalent bulk and nano-sized compounds are comparable in value: 166 J/kg vs. 175 J/kg (4 T) for bulk and nano-sized with x = 0.02 This is due to the wide effective temperature range of entropy change δTFWHM in nanocrystalline samples. All values of RCP are high and comparable with relevant compounds reported in the literature. Bulk samples with x = 0.3 exhibits positive entropy change at antiferromagnetic-ferromagnetic transition temperature Magnetic entropy changes and magnetic parameters of the bulk polycrystalline samples indicate them as potential candidates for magnetocaloric materials. Possibly, they can be combined in construction of multistep refrigeration processes to increase their temperature range and effectiveness. The nanocrystalline samples, which show comparatively lower maximum entropy change are moved to the immediate background of the picture of usable magnetocaloric compounds but could, possibly, be still useful in future developments.

Many high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) based on ferromagnetic (FM) 3d transition elements Co, Fe, and Ni are soft ferromagnets [, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ], possessing very narrow magnetization hysteresis loop, and in some cases also vanishing magnetostriction [, , ], where the FM material does not change its size and shape in an external magnetic field. The materials with this combination of magnetic properties are energy‐efficient in alternating‐current (ac) electromagnetic applications because the hysteresis losses are brought to minimum, while the vanishing magnetostriction implies that the material does not mechanically vibrate in an ac magnetic field and hence does not emit humming noise in the audio‐frequency range that can be annoying to a human ear. Such materials are “supersilent” in ac applications such as transformer cores, stators of electromotors, magnetocaloric coolers, and magnetocaloric heat pumps. chosen.technique: magnetometry and microcalorimetry on thickness‐series FeMnNiGeSi films
chosen.conditions: magnetocaloric measurements performed at multiple thicknesses (20–200 nm) in low‐field cycling (up to ~2 T) over 80–350 K
chosen.why: This approach most directly tests whether the bulk magnetocaloric response persists in low‐dimensional forms by examining how thickness and nanoscale structure affect the mechanism. Varying thin‐film thickness is a standard method in materials science to isolate finite‐size and interface effects on magnetic and caloric properties.
